Names the source, or deletes the claim.

brief.intro: It scans for the patterns below, then rewrites, keeping the meaning and the intended tone. Rule numbers are fixed ids other skills cite. The list gives one line per rule, from empty -ing phrases, AI words and dashes to chatbot phrases, metaphor nouns and passive voice.

lessons.quote: Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite.
lessons.quoteTr: Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite.
lessons.title: Give each rule a fixed number
lessons.does: Other skills can just say "apply rule 13", and the numbers still line up after rules are added or removed.
lessons.why: Fixed numbers make references short and exact, and they don't shift when the list changes.
lessons.try: Number your team's writing rules, then say in a review: "This paragraph breaks rule 4."

lessons.quote: Name the actor unless it is unknown or doesn't matter.
lessons.quoteTr: Name the actor unless it is unknown or doesn't matter.
lessons.title: Write the exception into the rule
lessons.does: It rewrites passive sentences to name who acts, and keeps the passive only when the actor is unknown or doesn't matter.
lessons.why: Stating the exception inside the rule stops the AI from rewriting every passive sentence, including the ones that should stay.
lessons.try: Put the exception in the request: "Give every paragraph a subheading, except paragraphs of one or two sentences."

lessons.quote: Cut a sentence that could appear unchanged in another project's docs.
lessons.quoteTr: Cut a sentence that could appear unchanged in another project's docs.
lessons.title: Test filler by moving it
lessons.does: Sentences that would fit any project get cut; what stays is about this project.
lessons.why: "Filler" is hard to judge, but "would it still fit elsewhere?" is a quick test anyone can run.
lessons.try: When you ask for an intro edit, add: "Delete any sentence that stays true with a competitor's name in it."

lessons.quote: One name per thing. Repeat it.
lessons.quoteTr: One name per thing. Repeat it.
lessons.title: Say repetition is fine
lessons.does: It calls one thing by one word from start to finish instead of cycling through synonyms for variety.
lessons.why: "Repeat it" gives explicit permission, so the AI stops renaming one thing until readers think it is several.
lessons.try: When you ask for an edit, add: "Call it 'order' everywhere. Don't switch to 'purchase' or 'transaction'."

blocks: Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.
Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.

3. No trailing "-ing" phrases that add no fact ("highlighting...", "ensuring...").
5. No vague attributions ("experts believe"). Name the source or delete.
7. No AI vocabulary: additionally, crucial, delve, enhance, foster, landscape, pivotal, showcase, testament, underscore, vibrant.
8. Say "is" or "has", not "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features".
9. No "not just X, but Y". State the point.
10. Don't force ideas into threes.
11. One name per thing. Repeat it.
12. No "from X to Y" unless X and Y sit on a real scale.
13. No em dashes, en dashes, or hyphens used as dashes, and no parentheses in their place. Use a period or a comma.
14. A colon goes before a list or an example, never mid-sentence as a connector.
15. Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. No bold label and colon that restates its line ("**Performance:** Performance improved..."). A bold lead-in that ends in a period and adds new detail is fine.
17. Sentence case headings.
18. No decorative emojis.
19. Straight quotes.
20. No chatbot phrases ("I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...").
22. No praise or agreement openers. Respond directly.
23. Cut filler. "In order to" becomes "to". Delete "it is important to note that".
24. One hedge at most: "may".
25. No generic conclusions. State specific plans or facts.
26. No abstract metaphor nouns: substrate, wedge, vector, nexus, primitive, harness, surface, scaffolding, paradigm, ratchet, north star, flywheel. Use the concrete word.
27. Say what it does, not how it feels. Name the mechanism or the number. Cut a sentence that could appear unchanged in another project's docs.
28. One idea per sentence. Split a sentence the reader has to reread.
29. Active voice. Name the actor unless it is unknown or doesn't matter.
30. Cut adverbs or use a stronger verb. Give the number.
31. Use the plain word: "use", not "utilize" or "leverage".
32. No metaphor, aphorism, personified code, or figurative verb where a literal phrase exists.
33. Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs. Spell out arrows and abbreviations.
